title: The cardinal-preservation proof uses an invalid supremum bound at singular cardinals.
details:
Spencer Unger, Forcing Summer School Lecture Notes, UCLA 2013, dated 2013-07-15, section13, Lemma13.1, printed/PDF p.39. Type: invalid inference in the written proof of a true theorem. After producing countable potential-value sets X_beta for beta<alpha<kappa, the proof claims that sup_{beta<alpha} sup X_beta is below kappa. This does not follow for singular kappa: take kappa=aleph_omega, alpha=omega and X_n={aleph_n}; each X_n is countable, but the displayed supremum equals kappa. Even the pointwise strict inequality f(beta)<sup X_beta needs a successor correction when X_beta has a maximum; that correction does not repair the singular-cardinal issue.

Repair: work inside M and bound the cardinality of X=union_{beta<alpha} X_beta by max(aleph_0,|alpha|)<kappa for uncountable cardinal kappa. Since every generic function value lies in its corresponding X_beta, X is a ground-model subset of kappa of size less than kappa and cannot contain the range of a surjection onto kappa. Handle finite and countable cardinals separately using ordinal/finite absoluteness. This is the union-cardinality argument in Marks, Set Theory, revision2026-01-31, Theorem26.2, p.104.

Corpus disposition: forcing-chain-conditions#cardinal-preservation adopts the repaired union-cardinality proof, explicitly handling finite and countable cardinals separately; #singular-bound-question explains why an unbounded union below a singular cardinal does not defeat the cardinality estimate. The theorem that ccc forcing preserves cardinals remains valid. The finding concerns only the 2013 edition, not the separately registered 2014 notes.
